title: The relative restriction kernel ideal is square-zero
statement: For a scheme X and ideal sheaves J ≤ I with I*I ≤ J, the kernel ideal of the section restriction map from the J-subscheme etale structure presheaf to the pullback along the inclusion of the I-subscheme has square-zero product on every etale object V.

proof.text: Set i = IdealSheafData.inclusion hJI. Its composite with J.subschemeι is I.subschemeι, hence map_ker and ker_subschemeι give i.ker.map J.subschemeι = I. The proved source-library theorem comap_map_of_isClosedImmersion recovers i.ker by pulling this equality back along J.subschemeι. Thus i.ker = I.comap J.subschemeι, the ideal I/J on the J-subscheme.

Use the proved source-library theorem IdealSheafData.comap_mul to rewrite the square of I.comap J.subschemeι as (I*I).comap J.subschemeι. Monotonicity carries hII into an inclusion in J.comap J.subschemeι, which is bottom by the proved comap_subschemeι. Consequently i.ker*i.ker ≤ bottom.

On the etale test object V, the structure-presheaf comparison is the appTop map of p = pullback.fst V.unop.hom i. Mathlib ker_fst_of_isClosedImmersion identifies p.ker with i.ker.comap V.unop.hom. Apply comap_mul, comap_mono, and comap_bot to the preceding square-zero inclusion to get p.ker*p.ker ≤ bottom.

The private, completely proved helper square_zero_global_kernel passes from this ideal-sheaf inclusion to global sections. By Ideal.mul_le it suffices to show a*b = 0 for two global kernel sections. At each point choose an affine open U. Naturality of p.app shows that the restrictions of a and b lie in RingHom.ker (p.app U).hom, which equals p.ker.ideal U by Hom.ker_apply since p is a closed immersion and therefore quasi-compact. Ideal.mul_mem_mul and the square-zero ideal-sheaf inclusion make their product zero on U. The scheme sheaf separatedness theorem Presheaf.IsSheaf.section_ext then gives a*b = 0 globally.

proof_origin.place: Proof, Step 1 and its Claim; implemented using the proved source-library ideal-sheaf pullback identities, with affine restriction and sheaf separatedness for global sections (2026-10-13).
